facts.statement: ELEC0031 Topic 8 is "Semiconductor III–V nanostructures".
Nanotechnology is the understanding and control of matter at dimensions of roughly 1 to 100 nm, where unique properties emerge that enable new technologies and products.
At the nanoscale, physical, chemical and biological properties differ from those of single atoms and of everyday-sized matter.

On the nanometre scale: water ~0.1 nm, glucose ~1 nm, an antibody ~10 nm, a virus ~100 nm, bacteria ~1 µm, a cancer cell ~10 µm, a full stop ~1 mm (10⁶ nm), a tennis ball ~10⁸ nm; nanodevices include nanopores, dendrimers, nanotubes, quantum dots and nanoshells.
Typical sizes: a bulk (volume) semiconductor ~1 cm; a waveguide ~1 µm, the wavelength of light; a quantum dot ~10 nm, the de Broglie wavelength of electrons at 300 K; an atom ~1 Å.
Large crystals have continuous band structure; as the size falls to the de Broglie wavelength the bands break up into the discrete levels of an atom.
The Schrödinger equation separates as Ψ(x,t) = ψ(x)T(t), with ∇²ψ + (2m/ħ²)(E − V)ψ = 0 and T(t) = e^(−iEt/ħ); ψ is the wavefunction, m the electron mass, E the total energy and V the potential.
In one dimension: d²ψ/dx² + (2m/ħ²)(E − V)ψ = 0.
Free electrons (V = 0): ψ(x) = A·e^(ikx) with k = √(2mE/ħ²), so E = ħ²k²/2m, a parabola in k: a continuum of energies, as in bulk material.
Infinite square well: V = 0 for 0 < x < L and V = ∞ outside; the particle is free inside and completely excluded outside.
Inside the well d²ψ/dx² + (2m/ħ²)Eψ = 0, with general solution ψ = A·e^(ikx) + B·e^(−ikx), or equivalently A·sin kx + B·cos kx, k = √(2mE/ħ²).
The boundary conditions ψ(0) = ψ(L) = 0 give B = 0 and A·sin kL = 0, so k = nπ/L with n = 1, 2, 3… (n = 0 would mean no particle).
facts.corrects: The slide writes k = ±nπ/L and calls these "bonding conditions". They are boundary conditions, and −n gives the same state as n, so n = 1, 2, 3…

facts.statement: ψₙ(x) = Aₙ sin(nπx/L) and Eₙ = n²π²ħ²/(2mL²): only discrete energies, the energy levels.
Normalising, ∫₀ᴸ Aₙ² sin²(nπx/L) dx = Aₙ²·L/2 = 1, so Aₙ = √(2/L).
For a 10 nm infinite well with the free-electron mass the levels are about 3.8, 15, 34, 60 and 94 meV for n = 1–5; ψₙ has n − 1 nodes inside the well and |ψₙ|² has n peaks.
A quantum well confines particles that were free to move in three dimensions to two dimensions, a planar region.
Quantum confinement appears when the well thickness becomes comparable to the de Broglie wavelength of the carriers (electrons and holes), giving discrete energy levels called energy subbands.

Bulk A, B and A each have their own band edges; grown as epitaxial layers A (50 nm) / B (5 nm) / A (50 nm), the narrow-gap B forms a quantum well with discrete levels in both the conduction and valence bands.
Infinite well: energy is quantised, and even the lowest level has a positive energy.
Infinite well: the particle can only be found with the energy of one of the levels, never in between.
Infinite well: when L is very large, Eₙ and Eₙ₊₁ become close and the system becomes classical, with continuous energy.
Finite well (barrier height U₀): the wavefunction is not zero at the walls but decays into the barriers.
Finite-well energy levels lie below the infinite-well levels of the same width.
The deeper the finite well, the better the infinite well approximates its low-lying levels.
In a finite well quantum-mechanical tunnelling is possible: the particle has a non-zero probability of being in (and through) the barrier.
Type-I heterostructure: the band gap of one material lies entirely within the wider gap of the other, so electrons and holes fall into wells in the same layer, which makes recombination efficient.

Type-II heterostructure: the gaps are staggered so the conduction-band minimum and valence-band maximum are in different materials; electrons and holes are confined in different layers and their recombination times are long.
The sketches: B/A/B is type I (e⁻ and hole both in A); C/A/C is type II with the electron in A and the hole in C; D/A/D is type II with the electron in D and the hole in A.
A quantum wire is confined in only two dimensions: it has length, along which electrons propagate particle-like.
Quantum wire (cross-section a × b, infinite walls): ψ(x,y,z) = e^(ik_x x)·√(2/a) sin(nπy/a)·√(2/b) sin(lπz/b).
facts.corrects: The slide uses n in both sine factors; the z factor carries its own quantum number l, matching the energy formula.

facts.statement: Wire energies: E = ħ²k_x²/2m + ħ²n²π²/(2ma²) + ħ²l²π²/(2mb²), with n, l = 1, 2, 3…
facts.corrects: The slide lists the quantum numbers as ±1, ±2, ±3…; a standing wave sin(−nπx/a) = −sin(nπx/a) is the same state, so each number runs over 1, 2, 3… only.

facts.statement: Quantum dots ("quantum boxes", "artificial atoms") are confined in all three dimensions and have discrete energy levels; the focus is on their optical properties, though their electronic transport is interesting too.
Quantum dot (a × b × c, infinite walls): ψ = √(2/a) sin(nπx/a)·√(2/b) sin(lπy/b)·√(2/c) sin(jπz/c).
facts.corrects: The slide uses n in all three sine factors; each direction has its own quantum number (n, l, j), as in the energy formula.

facts.statement: Dot energies: E = (ħ²π²/2m)(n²/a² + l²/b² + j²/c²), with n, l, j = 1, 2, 3…
facts.corrects: The slide lists the quantum numbers as ±1, ±2, ±3…; a standing wave sin(−nπx/a) = −sin(nπx/a) is the same state, so each number runs over 1, 2, 3… only.

facts.statement: Quantum wells are made by epitaxy: TEM cross-sections of InGaAs/GaAs and InGaAs/InAlAs quantum wells show the thin well layers as sharp stripes (50 nm scale bar).

The two simplest ways to confine electrons in two dimensions: (a) etching an A/B/A quantum-well layer into a narrow ridge; (b) split gates on top, which deplete the well everywhere except under the gap between them.

Vapour–liquid–solid (VLS) growth (Wagner and Ellis, 1964): a catalyst droplet (Au) is deposited, forms a liquid Au–Ga eutectic, Ga and As supersaturate it and GaAs nucleates beneath it, and the nanowire grows up under the droplet; growth on the side walls tapers it.
VLS nanowires are grown bottom-up by direct epitaxy with metal (Au) seeds or self-catalysed (Ga) seeds.
Quantum-dot fabrication engineers potential-energy barriers that confine electrons in three dimensions, by three primary methods: lithography, colloidal chemistry and epitaxy.

Lithographic dots: pillars are etched (after electron-beam lithography) in a quantum-well heterostructure; the well’s band-gap mismatch gives confinement in one dimension and the pillar walls the other two.
Lithographic dots’ disadvantages: slow, contamination, low density and defect formation (etch-induced surface damage on the pillar walls).
The pillar: GaAs / AlGaAs / InGaAs / AlGaAs / GaAs on a GaAs substrate, with InGaAs the well.

Colloidal dots: reactions are engineered to precipitate quantum dots from solution or a host (e.g. a polymer); the surface sometimes needs "capping" with bonded molecules to stay chemically stable; core–shell structures are possible; materials are typically II–VI (CdS, CdSe).
Colloidal dots vary in size ("size dispersion").
CdSe-core / ZnS-shell dots glow red when bigger and blue when smaller: stronger confinement raises the transition energy.
Patterned growth: QDs are grown in pyramid-shaped recesses formed by selective ion etching (Fukui et al.: GaAs tetrahedral dots in AlGaAs by selective-area MOCVD on (111)B GaAs through an SiO₂ mask).
Patterned growth’s disadvantage: the density of QDs is limited by the mask pattern.
Self-organised dots form through epitaxial strain in the Stranski–Krastanov mode (by MBE or MOCVD): islands, tens of nm in size, form on a wetting layer because of the lattice mismatch.
Self-organised dots’ disadvantages: size and shape fluctuations, and their ordering.
Island initiation can be controlled by inducing local strain, growing on dislocations, varying growth conditions, or combining with patterning.
AFM images of islands on GaAs: (a) InAs islands nucleated at random; (b) a random distribution of ring-shaped InGaAs islands; (c) a 2D lattice of InAs islands.
Higher-quality quantum dots are made by MBE, thanks to its precise control of deposited thickness and its low growth rate compared with MOCVD and CVD.
In InAs/GaAs the initial 2D layer transforms into 3D islands typically 2–10 nm high and 20–40 nm wide.
InAs/GaAs dots are imaged in cross-section by STM and TEM (stacked dot layers, 50 nm bar) and in plan view by AFM (200 nm bar).
The density of states is the number of electron states per unit volume per unit energy: ρ(E) = (1/V)·dN/dE.
With 3, 2, 1 and 0 degrees of freedom the density of states goes as E^(1/2), E⁰ (constant), E^(−1/2) and δ(E).
In 3D each allowed state takes a k-space volume (π/a)(π/b)(π/c) = π³/V, and the states with energy below E fill a sphere of volume 4πk³/3, with k = √(2mE/ħ²).
3D count: N = (4πk³/3)/(π³/V) × 2 (two spins) × ⅛ (only positive k_x, k_y, k_z: ± give the same standing wave) = k³V/(3π²).
2D (quantum well): each state takes π²/A of k-space and the states fill a circle πk², so N = (πk²)/(π²/A) × 2 × ¼ = k²A/(2π).
2D: N = mAE/(πħ²), so ρ(E) = m/(πħ²), independent of energy; right at the band edge a large number of states is available.
1D (quantum wire): each state takes π/L of k-space and the states fill the line from −k to +k, length 2k, so N = (2k/(π/L)) × 2 × ½ = 2kL/π.
facts.corrects: The slide takes the line’s length as k but still applies the ½ for ± redundancy, counting each state half; with the line from −k to +k (as the full sphere and circle are used in 3D and 2D) N = 2kL/π.
The slide gives ρ(E) = (1/2π)√(2m/ħ²)E^(−1/2), half the correct value, because of the N = kL/π count on slide 28. Counting standing waves k = nπ/L directly (n = 1, 2, 3…, two spins) gives N = 2kL/π.

facts.statement: 0D (quantum dot): no free motion, so there is no k-space to fill and states exist only at discrete energies: ρ(E) = 2δ(E − E_c) for each level, the 2 counting spin.
facts.corrects: The slide writes ρ(E) = 2σ(E − E_c). The function is the Dirac delta, δ, as the slide’s own text says.

facts.statement: On one energy axis (0–120 meV) the bulk DoS is a √E curve, the well a staircase stepping up at each subband, the wire a spike falling as 1/√E at each subband, and the dot isolated delta lines.
Quantum dots give narrow emission spectra because of their δ-function density of states.
The large energy separation between the ground and excited states makes it hard to excite carriers thermally out of the ground state, which promises temperature-independent lasing.
The active volume of quantum dots is very small, so a very low threshold current is expected for QD lasers.
Single-photon devices, quantum-dot infrared photodetectors (QDIPs) and solar cells are also being investigated with quantum dots.
Advantages of the QD laser: a low threshold current density and stable operation.
The QD laser: an n⁺ GaAs substrate and buffer, Al₀.₃Ga₀.₇As cladding, GaAs, dots in In₀.₄Ga₀.₆As, GaAs and Al₀.₃Ga₀.₇As cladding, shaped as a ridge about 1 mm long.

In power–current curves the QD Fabry–Pérot laser keeps an almost constant threshold current and slope efficiency from −40 °C to +100 °C, while conventional quantum-well lasers’ thresholds rise and slopes fall as they heat up.
